title: 12 Classroom Management Myths You Need To Know About d-to-know-about/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin lists twelve widely-held classroom management beliefs he considers myths, each paired with an explanation of the more effective alternative. Examples include the idea that teachers shouldn't smile early in the year (he says a smile builds rapport instead), that kindness invites students to take advantage (only failing to follow through does that), and that too much fun causes misbehavior (he argues the opposite is true). Other myths addressed include over-praising expected behavior, needing tougher rather than better-enforced consequences, relying on rewards, sending students to the office, lecturing individual students, and believing that classroom quality depends on the roster rather than the teacher. He closes by reiterating that building classroom community results from consistent accountability and shared enjoyment rather than being a direct goal to pursue.
points: Smiling and building rapport early in the year helps, rather than hurts, classroom management—being stern limits a teacher's influence.
Toughening consequences isn't necessary; strengthening existing ones through classroom leverage and enjoyment is what matters.
Praising students for merely expected behavior lowers the bar and undercuts the meaning of genuine praise.
Sending students to the office or lecturing them individually both weaken a teacher's authority and increase resentment.
Classroom community is a byproduct of consistent accountability and shared enjoyment, not something pursued directly.
quotes: Your smile should be the first thing students notice about you. It sets the tone for the new school year and gives you a jumpstart on building rapport.
Students will only take advantage of you if you say you’re going to hold them accountable and you don’t.
If students are having fun learning in your classroom, your rules and consequences will have more power to dissuade misbehavior.
Praising students for expected behavior sends the message that doing what you’re supposed to do deserves special recognition.
You don’t need tougher consequences. You just need to strengthen the ones you have. You do this by creating a classroom that students want to be a part of.
Sending students to the office weakens your ability to manage your classroom. It communicates to your students that the buck doesn’t stop with you.
You decide whether you have a good class or not, not the students. You have the power to create the class you want, regardless of who is on your roster.
